Sample text:
---
The book was red, the red of a fire truck seen through rain, and it smelled like pencil shavings and the inside of an old piano. I found it on the bottom shelf of the used bookstore, wedged between a field guide to mushrooms and a biography of a statesman nobody remembered. When I opened it, a piece of paper slipped out and landed on my shoe. It was a list, written in careful looped handwriting, numbered from one to twelve.

1. Learn the name of the moon in another language.
2. Apologize to the tree on Ninth Street.
3. Buy a stranger’s coffee without letting them know.
4. Walk home by a route you have never taken.
5. Write a letter to the person you were at seventeen.
6. Sit with the discomfort of a cloudy afternoon.
7. Learn the difference between loneliness and solitude.
8. Call your grandmother even if she is gone.
9. Eat a peach over the sink.
10. Tell the truth about something small.
11. Stand at the edge of a river and do not take a photograph.
12. Forgive the version of yourself who could not do any of this yet.

I read the list twice. The handwriting looked familiar in the way a stranger’s face sometimes looks familiar: not because you know them, but because you have been waiting to meet someone like them. The bookstore owner was behind the counter, sorting paperbacks into a cardboard box. I asked if he knew whose book this had been. He glanced at the cover, shrugged, and said, “People leave things in books. It’s practically a library service.” Then he went back to sorting, as if the whole world were a matter of moving one object from one box to another.

Outside, the afternoon was doing that thing where the light turns the sidewalks the color of weak tea. I put the list in my pocket and walked without deciding where to go. I passed the tree on Ninth Street. It was an old maple, or maybe a sycamore; I am not good with trees. Someone had carved initials into it long ago, and the bark had healed around the letters like a scar that had decided to become decorative. I stopped and said, “I’m sorry.” I did not know what I was apologizing for. For the nails people hammer into trees? For the way I had never noticed it before? For all the things I had used without thanking? The tree did not answer. A breeze moved through its branches, and a few leaves came loose and spun down like small, green envelopes with no addresses.

At the coffee shop on the corner, a man in a gray coat was counting coins on the counter. He was short by sixty cents. The barista was already reaching for the register, kind and tired, but I stepped forward and paid. The man looked at me, surprised. “Thanks,” he said. “I’ll get you back.” I told him not to. He asked my name anyway, and I told him, and he said, “I’m Gerald. I’m going to remember that.” I don’t know if he did. I don’t need him to. I sat by the window and watched the street perform its ordinary miracle: people moving past one another, carrying invisible burdens, deciding every few seconds whether to be kind. The list in my pocket felt warm, as if it had been waiting for me to catch up with it.

That night I wrote to my seventeen-year-old self. I told them: You will not believe how quiet the future can be. You will not believe how much of it is just laundry and grocery lists and deciding what to eat. You will fall in love with people who do not love you back, and you will survive it. You will learn that being liked is not the same as being known. You will stop wanting to be impressive and start wanting to be honest. You will still be afraid of the dark, but you will learn to leave a light on and call that courage. I folded the letter and put it in a drawer. I did not send it anywhere. There is no postage for time.

On Sunday I walked home by a route I had never taken. I went past a community garden where tomatoes hung like small red lanterns, past a house with a piano on the porch and a sign that said FREE TO A GOOD HOME, past a mural of a woman holding a bowl of stars. I got slightly lost. I stood at the edge of a river I did not know was there. The water was brown and silver at once, carrying the sky in pieces. I took out my phone, then put it away. I stood there until my feet went cold. I did not name the moon in another language. I did not call my grandmother, because she is gone, and the phone does not have a number for that kind of silence. But I stood still, and I forgave myself for the years I spent running from quiet rooms. Then I walked home, and I ate a peach over the sink, and the juice ran down my wrist like something sweet and temporary, like a summer that knows it is almost over.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: VARY

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW. A lyrical first-person story turns a found list into a sequence of small acts of attention and forgiveness.

## Grounded reading
The voice is intimate, sensory, and gently wistful, finding emotional weight in ordinary things: a worn book, a tree scarred by initials, coins on a counter, laundry, a peach. Its pathos is quiet rather than tragic; the narrator is learning to stop running from silence and to be kinder to past and present selves. The list gives the piece a simple structure, but the narrator’s imperfect follow-through makes its invitation feel human: pay attention, try small acts of care, and forgive yourself for what you cannot do.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample foregrounds everyday kindness, noticing the world without documenting it, and accepting that some losses cannot be repaired by a phone call or a letter. Its recurring objects—the list, the tree, the river, and the peach—make ordinary gestures feel like modest rituals. The moral emphasis is on honesty and self-forgiveness, not on becoming impressive or completing every task.

## Evidence line
> There is no postage for time.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the sample sustains a distinctive, coherent lyric voice, with recurring imagery and emotional concerns woven through its narrative resolution.
